summary: For ages 9–10 (UK Year 5 Forces), teach the qualitative big idea that levers, pulleys and gears let a smaller force have a greater effect — and that this is not free, but a trade: you apply a smaller force but must move the effort end a greater distance. Anchor in real measurement (force meters, a rigid ruler/rod, masses, a movable pivot) using predict-then-measure, supported where helpful by an on-screen workbench that recomputes effort live as the pivot moves. Name load, effort and pivot/fulcrum, cover all three mechanisms and what each changes, and connect to everyday objects to challenge 'all levers work the same' and over-narrow images of pulleys and gears. Reserve quantitative moment = force × distance for later (KS3).
misconceptions: 'All levers work the same way' (Oak) — children miss that pivot position and effort-vs-load placement change how much effort is needed.
Thinking a machine creates extra force from nothing — missing the force-for-distance trade-off.
'Gears only exist in bicycles and cars' (Oak) — not recognising gears more widely.
'All pulleys have the wheel fixed to a ceiling' (Oak) — over-narrow image of a pulley.
Confusing which part is the effort and which is the load, especially in second/third-class arrangements (wheelbarrow, tweezers).

activities.title: Measure the effort drop on a real lever (predict-then-measure)
steps: Set up a stiff ruler or rod across a movable pivot (e.g. a pencil or small log), with a fixed mass as the load near one end.
Before testing, predict: as you move the pivot toward the load (and apply the effort further from the pivot), will the effort needed go up or down — and why? Write or say your prediction.
Hook a force meter at the effort end (or push and feel the effort) and read the effort needed to lift the fixed load with the pivot in its first position.
Slide the pivot closer to the load, repeat the measurement, and record how the force-meter reading changes.
Notice and describe what your hand/the effort end has to do: how far it moves compared with how far the load rises.
activities.insight: As the pivot moves closer to the load, so that the effort is applied further from the pivot than the load is, the effort needed to lift a fixed load drops. A smaller force has a greater effect, but the effort end travels a longer distance. You apply a smaller force at the cost of moving further. The lever does not create energy: the bigger force on the load is paid for by your end moving further.

activities.title: On-screen mechanism workbench: drag the pivot and watch effort change
steps: On a lever workbench, try to lift a heavy crate; read the force-meter with the pivot in the middle — the reading is high because, with equal distances either side of the pivot, the push needed is about the same as the load's weight (it needs a big push).
Predict what will happen to the effort, then drag the pivot toward the crate and watch the effort reading fall as the same load lifts under a gentler push.
Observe the ghosted 'effort arc' showing the effort end sweeping through a longer path — name the bargain: less force, more distance.

Switch to pulley mode: thread an extra movable (supporting) wheel to build toward a block-and-tackle and watch the effort reading fall; note that a single fixed wheel would only change the direction you pull, while a movable wheel reduces the effort.
Switch to gear mode: mesh a small driver gear into a large gear and describe what happens to force and to speed/direction.
activities.insight: The live recompute of the effort meter as the pivot/pulley/gears change makes 'a smaller force has a greater effect' something the child drives and sees, including the force-for-distance trade shown as a longer effort arc. A fixed pulley changes direction; a movable pulley reduces effort.

activities.title: Name the parts and classify everyday machines
steps: On a lever diagram, label the load (object being lifted), the effort (force you apply) and the pivot/fulcrum (fixed point it turns on) — learn 'pivot' and 'fulcrum' as the same thing.
Sort everyday objects into lever, pulley or gear: seesaw, crowbar, scissors, wheelbarrow, bottle opener, tweezers, the elbow joint, egg-whisk, flagpole pulley.
For each lever example, mark where the effort, load and pivot are — including trickier arrangements like the wheelbarrow and tweezers.

Match each mechanism to what it changes: a lever reduces the effort when the effort is further from the pivot than the load is (e.g. crowbar, bottle opener, wheelbarrow), but some levers, such as tweezers and the elbow, need a larger effort in exchange for a bigger, faster or more precise movement at the load; a pulley changes direction and (with an extra movable wheel) reduces effort; gears change the size and/or direction of the turning force and the speed of turning.
Answer prediction prompts such as: 'Move the pivot toward the load — does the effort go up or down?'
activities.insight: Grounding the abstraction in familiar objects, and correctly locating effort/load/pivot even in awkward arrangements, consolidates the vocabulary and challenges over-narrow images (gears only in bikes/cars; pulleys only fixed overhead).

activities.title: Build-and-test extension: gear trains and a block-and-tackle
steps: Assemble a simple gear train with different-sized cogs and turn the driver; observe which gear turns faster and which turns with more force.
Rig a real pulley with a string and hanging load, then add a movable wheel to build a simple block-and-tackle; feel the effort change and note any change in pull direction.
Describe how the physical assembly (spacing, meshing, number of supporting ropes) affects what the mechanism does.
activities.insight: Physically assembling mechanisms adds tangibility and an engineering feel, letting children see how real spacing and meshing produce the force/direction/speed changes modelled elsewhere.

checkQuestion: A child can't lift a heavy rock by hand, but by pushing down on the far end of a long strong bar resting on a small log, they lift it easily. How does the bar let them lift something they couldn't lift on their own — and are they getting the lift for free?
checkAnswer: It's a lever: the log is the pivot (fulcrum), the rock is the load, the child's push is the effort. Pushing far from the pivot lets a small effort move a big load — a smaller force has a greater effect. It isn't free: the child's end moves a LONGER way (and pushes down further) than the rock rises — the machine trades distance for force, it doesn't create energy.
